notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Habakkuk 3, drawn only from the pages I read. A few things to know about the coverage first:

- I didn't find any pages on Habakkuk 3 from the Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox sites, or from bibleodyssey.org.
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so that section is left out.
- The NET Bible notes appear only where preceptaustin.org quotes them. I didn't read netbible.org itself.
- "Tradition" points mostly come from older commentators whose church background is widely known (Calvin and Barnes: Reformed/Presbyterian; Benson: Methodist; Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary: Anglican; Gill: Baptist). The labels are my own; the sources don't state them. Where traditions differ here, it's mainly about the interpretation of one verse (v. 13), not along denominational lines.

**Overview**
- Guzik's outline: a plea for revival (vv. 1–2), a song about God's power (vv. 3–15), then rejoicing in the Lord even if everything else collapses (vv. 16–19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- Ellicott calls vv. 1–15 a hymn about a *future* appearance of God on Israel's behalf, with the same signs and wonders as Israel's early history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Pulpit says the imagery comes from Egypt, the Red Sea, Sinai, the Jordan and Canaan. Habakkuk treats these as previews of God's final work, setting up the Messiah's kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 1**
- NET note (quoted on Precept Austin): nobody knows what "Shigionoth" means. It may name the type of poem or the musical style. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary
- Ellicott: it's called a "prayer" rather than a psalm because it describes a rescue that faith expects through prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Poole (quoted on biblehub) mentions an older view that Shigionoth means "ignorances": the prophet admitting his errors and asking pardon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/3-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: revival is God's work, not man's. Our part is to cry out for it. We should pray "revive *Your* work," not our own, and also "revive me." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- Guzik: "In wrath remember mercy" admits the people deserve God's anger, so they can only ask for mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- Ellicott: God's acts at the beginning of Israel's history are well known; the prophet asks to see them again "in the midst of the years." The plea for mercy means: the punishment is deserved, but limit how long it lasts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Ryrie (quoted on Precept Austin) reads "revive" as asking God to carry out His announced plan of judgment on Judah, and then on Babylon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary
- **Catholic reading:** The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "between two living creatures you shall be known." Haydock says this was read as Christ found "between an ox and an ass." He adds that the tradition of two animals at the manger is no older than about the fifth century, and that modern scholars follow Jerome's translation instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/habakkuk-3.html
- **Protestant view of the same reading:** Gill (Baptist) calls it a mistranslation and a wrong sense. Still, he grants it holds an old truth: the passage is about God's work in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kja/habakkuk/3-2.html
- Pulpit lists other readings of the Greek, such as "two lives" (this life and the next) or Christ's life before and after the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: this echoes Moses' description of God appearing at Sinai (Deut 33:2; Judg 5:4). As God came then to make a covenant, He will come again to rescue and judge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- Ellicott: the old King James Version wrongly puts all these verbs in the past tense. They describe a future scene that faith sees as already present. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Teman means Edom to the southeast; Paran is the mountain region to the southwest. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/3-3.htm
- Guzik: while praying for revival, Habakkuk starts praising the God who sends it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- **End-times reading:** Henry Morris (quoted on Precept Austin) says part of this refers to the Exodus and Sinai, but the events after the "Selah" will literally happen when Christ returns after the Great Tribulation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary
- **Gospel-age reading:** Gill sees it as God's past help at Sinai, and also as a picture of the Messiah coming from Bethlehem or through the spread of the gospel after Pentecost. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/habakkuk-3.html

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: the brightness is sunlight. The "horns" from His hand are rays of light; Keil notes that Arabic poetry compares early sunrays to a gazelle's horns. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock cites the Septuagint wording about the "strong love of his power" and applies it to Jesus Christ, who gave His life for us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/habakkuk-3.html

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: plague goes ahead of God to punish His enemies (as in Egypt and Canaan) and the disobedient among His own people. The Septuagint has "word" where Hebrew has "pestilence." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- Ellicott (citing Kleinert) links these "angels of death" to the destruction of Sennacherib's army (2 Kings 19:35). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "His ways are everlasting" means He acts as He did of old, when He brought Israel out of Egypt. The mountains shake as Sinai did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Henderson (quoted in the Pulpit sermon notes): as God marches to rescue His people, He suddenly stops, and everything is thrown into terror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the image is probably still from the Exodus. Cushan (Cush) and Midian were peoples on either side of the Red Sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Pulpit: "I saw" means in a prophetic vision. The nations shake with fear as they did when they heard of the Exodus (Ex 15:14–16). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: the questions don't expect an answer; they add energy to the poem. God wasn't angry with nature. He was showing He rules creation and will save His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- Ellicott: this refers to crossing the Red Sea and the Jordan. God's "horses and chariots" contrast with Pharaoh's (Ex 14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Precept Austin: here the prophet stops describing God and speaks to Him directly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the bow is "bared," taken out of its case, a picture of God's sworn punishments. "Cleaving the earth with rivers" means new streams bursting from the rocks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET note on Precept Austin):** "split the earth" can sound like geology to us. In a thunderstorm scene it more likely means streams swollen into flash floods. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: this describes an earthquake, like Sinai shaking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- Ellicott: the background is Sinai and the Red Sea's waters standing up like walls. Such images are common in poems about God stepping in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Gill also reads the mountains as powerful nations and rulers, terrified by God's acts for His people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/habakkuk-3.html

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: this recalls Joshua 10:12–13. God's appearance is so bright that it shames the sun and moon, and they stop moving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: the Judge strides across the earth. This is a general statement, not limited to Joshua's conquest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 13 — the main disagreement: who is "Your anointed"?**
- **The Messiah:** Guzik says it is "none other than" Jesus Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- **The king, then the Messiah:** Pulpit (Anglican) says "anointed" always means one person, never the whole people. So it means the Davidic king first and the Messiah second. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- **God's chosen people:** Ellicott (Anglican) disagrees. He reads "the salvation of Your anointed," meaning Israel, as in Ps 105:15. He says few impartial Hebrew scholars would disagree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/3-13.htm
- **Christ, firmly:** Barnes (Presbyterian) backs the "with Your anointed" reading. He says "anointed" is never used of the people. He sees all of God's rescues pointing to Christ, and the "head of the house of the wicked" as Satan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/3-13.htm
- **The Messiah through earlier leaders:** JFB, citing Calvin (Reformed), says the Messiah, of whom Moses, Joshua and David were forerunners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/3-13.htm
- **Israel's leaders:** Benson (Methodist) says God's appointed leaders: Moses, Joshua, Samuel and David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/3-13.htm
- **Joshua as a picture of Jesus:** Matthew Henry says Joshua was a figure of Jesus, and calls the passage a picture of the world's redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/3-13.htm
- **Moses and Israel, pointing ahead:** MacArthur (quoted on Precept Austin) says it most likely means Moses and Israel at the Exodus, but ultimately points to a future rescue by the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary
- **"Head of the house of the wicked":** Ellicott says Babylon (the Chaldeans) will be destroyed "root and branch." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm Pulpit notes some see an echo of Gen 3:15 or of Jael killing Sisera. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: the first half is very obscure, and the Hebrew words can mean "spear/rod/tribe" and "princes/villages." The last part echoes Psalms 10, 14 and 17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Pulpit: the enemy are like the Chaldeans of 1:6. "Me" shows the prophet speaking as one of his people. "The poor" are Israel first, then all humble worshippers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: the Exodus is the model of God rescuing His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- Ellicott: "heap of great waters" is probably the right translation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: this is the right response to God's power, admitting one's own weakness. The prophet remembers that God will direct the Babylonian invasion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- **Two readings of the line about waiting:**
  - Pulpit: "I who shall rest," a sudden confidence that God's people will have rest.
  - Keil (cited by Pulpit): he trembles because he must sit still and wait for the day of trouble.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: better translated "For." The invasion will bring famine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/3.htm
- Pulpit: the Chaldeans cut down and burned fruit trees in lands they invaded. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/3-17.htm
- Calvin (Reformed): our joy will not depend on outward prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/3-17.html

**v. 18**
- Guzik: Habakkuk wasn't just practising positive thinking. He saw the problems clearly and remembered God was greater. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- Pulpit: "I will joy" means my joy will show outwardly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/habakkuk/3.htm
- Precept Austin: the Hebrew root behind "exult" carries the idea of circling, or dancing, for joy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary

**v. 19**
- Guzik: his strength is not in crops or flocks but in the Lord. The deer leaping on the hills means steady steps and joy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/habakkuk-3/
- Pulpit sermon notes: perhaps swiftness to escape danger, but also, as a general truth, eagerness in doing one's duty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/habakkuk/3.htm
- Precept Austin: the closing note shows Israel kept singing this psalm, including after the exile. https://www.preceptaustin.org/habakkuk_3_commentary
